extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant), especially those studying aesthetics and the Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explicating Kant's criteria for aesthetic (aesthetical) and teleological judgements — what makes a judgement of taste, the conditions of its validity, and how purposiveness relates to feeling and cognition. Suitable for readers analyzing Kantian aesthetics or applying his distinctions to judgments of beauty and teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: The judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judgement of taste is aesthetical" — its determining ground can be no other than subjective: it refers the representation to the subject and its feeling of pleasure or pain rather than to the Object for cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the difference between logical (objective) judgements and aesthetical ones: an aesthetical judgement compares a given representation with the subject's whole faculty of representations and refers it to pleasure/pain, adding nothing to cognition. Example contrast: apprehending a purposive building vs being conscious of satisfaction in that apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: "The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested" — the satisfaction relevant to judging something beautiful is not interest tied to desire or to the object's existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'interest' (satisfaction connected to desire or the object's existence) from the disinterested pleasure of taste. Kant gives examples (palace, cook-shops, Rousseau) to illustrate that aesthetic judgement suspends considerations of usefulness or desire; it asks only whether mere representation accompanies satisfaction, irrespective of existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in aesthetic judgement is grounded a priori and claims universal validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of pleasure in aesthetic judgement is "determined by a ground a priori and valid for every man" by reference of the object to cognitive faculties, even though the pleasure itself is not a concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the pleasure is empirical and not a concept, the judgement of taste claims universal validity because its ground lies in the universal (though subjective) conditions of reflective judgement — the harmony of Imagination with Understanding. Thus a judgement based on this pleasure can legitimately claim that everyone ought to agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic (formal/subjective) purposiveness vs logical (objective) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposiveness may be represented subjectively as the harmony of an object's form with the cognitive faculties (aesthetical/formal purposiveness) or objectively as the harmony of form with the possibility of the thing according to a concept (logical/real purposiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective purposiveness is tied to immediate pleasure in form (aesthetic experience) and does not ascribe properties to the object in itself; objective purposiveness concerns natural purposes and is judged by Understanding and Reason (teleological judgement). Kant uses this distinction to justify separating the Critique into aesthetical and teleological parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement bases pleasure on apprehension of form without reference to concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure relevant to taste arises when apprehension of the form of an object occurs "without reference to a concept for a definite cognition," i.e., the pleasure is in the form itself and not in conceptual understanding of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Imagination, in mere apprehension (apprehensio), may be placed in agreement with the Understanding, producing a feeling of pleasure. Such pleasure cannot be captured by concepts and thus grounds aesthetic (not cognitive) judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is the faculty of judging by means of pleasure grounded in harmony of Imagination and Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty whose judgements of beauty rest on a feeling of pleasure that arises from the conformity (harmony) of the Imagination with the Understanding in reflection, producing a representation of formal purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this harmony is a universal condition of reflective judgement (though subjective), the judgements of taste can legitimately claim a priori validity for everyone. Taste thus determines by feeling rather than by conceptual rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement is reflective, not determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between determinant and reflective judgement: determinant judgement subsumes a given representation under a concept, whereas reflective judgement seeks or prescribes a principle for given representations (it does not determine objects by concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflective judgement is the mode operative in aesthetics and teleology: it prescribes how to proceed in reflection upon objects (e.g., assuming purposiveness of nature for cognition) rather than applying pre-existing concepts to determine objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement contributes nothing to knowledge of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetical judgement "contributes nothing towards the knowledge of its objects"; it is concerned with critique of the judging subject and its faculties (feeling of pleasure/pain), not with constitutive cognitive claims about objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore aesthetic analysis belongs to the critique of the subject's faculties (propaedeutic of philosophy) rather than to theoretical doctrine aimed at cognition of objects. Use aesthetic judgement to assess subjective harmony, not to expand objective knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: The concept of purposiveness of nature is a transcendental, regulative principle for reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement presupposes a transcendental principle that nature is purposive for our cognitive faculties (a purposiveness of nature in relation to the reflective judgement), which must be assumed a priori to make connected experience possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is subjective (it prescribes to the Judgement) and is not a property learned from nature; it enables the Understanding to seek unity among empirical laws. It explains our adoption of maxims like that nature exhibits systematic unity helpful to cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement's claim to universality rests on subjective universal conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the pleasure in aesthetic judgement is empirical and singular, it "justly claims the agreement of every one" because the ground of the pleasure is found in the universal conditions of reflective judgement (purposive harmony of cognitive faculties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that this ground is not a conceptual rule but a shared structural feature of cognition (Imagination and Understanding), which permits the aesthetic judgement to appeal to universal assent despite its basis in feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Critique: aesthetical vs teleological judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant divides the Critique of Judgement into the Critique of aesthetical Judgement (formal purposiveness judged by feeling of pleasure/pain) and the Critique of teleological Judgement (real/objective purposiveness judged by Understanding and Reason).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetical judgement handles formal purposiveness (natural beauty) via taste and feeling; teleological judgement handles natural purposes (organised bodies, technic of nature) via conceptual judgement. The two use different faculties and yield different types of claims about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling of pleasure/pain is not an ingredient of cognition and cannot predicate properties of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation and space may serve as elements of cognition; but the subjective element in representation "which cannot be an ingredient of cognition" is the feeling of pleasure or pain — it signifies nothing about the object itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore aesthetic predicates (beauty, sublime) are not cognitive predicates of objects-in-themselves but indicate the subject's relation to the representation. When analyzing artworks or natural beauty, do not conflate aesthetic feeling with objective properties.
